_comment: Polynesian expansion batch 156 - Grey, Polynesian Mythology (1855), ch. 14 'The Emigration of Turi' (pp. 202-220): the Hawepotiki feud, Kupe's discovery voyage, and Turi's settlement at Patea. Topics 4 founding legends, 8 trickster, 9 sacred landscape. All passages are labeled paraphrase.

title.en: Turi's Feast of Hearts and the Overheard Lament
title.zh: 圖里復仇與被竊聽的哀歌

region.zh: 哈瓦基瓦雷庫拉大屋（象徵性定位）

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 14, The Emigration of Turi (London 1855)

summary.en: When the boy Potikiroroa trips in the doorway of Uenuku's sacred house - a fatal omen - the high priest devours him uncooked. Turi revenges him by luring Uenuku's little son Hawepotiki into the summer river and killing him, then smuggles the baked heart into the food-basket sent up to Uenuku, who eats it lamenting his missing child. 'Let it be; he lies in the belly of Toi-te-huatahi', he says - a proverb of dreadful revenge. Rongo-rongo overhears the war chant in Wharekura summoning the tribes to destroy Turi, and the flight that becomes the Aotea migration begins.
summary.zh: 男孩波蒂基羅羅阿在烏努庫聖屋門口絆倒——凶兆！大祭司竟將其生吞。圖里為友報仇：誘烏努庫幼子哈維波蒂基下河戲水而殺之，又將其烤熟的心臟混入敬獻烏努庫的食籃；烏努庫食畢方知吃了愛子，卻只道『罷了；他躺在圖伊特胡阿塔希的肚腹裡』——此諺意為必報大仇。妻子龍戈龍戈竊得瓦雷庫拉中召喚諸部滅圖里的戰歌，遂啟逃亡——此即奧特亞號遷徙之始。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection; cannibal revenge episode reproduced as paraphrase.

passages.text: Hoiraatua, a near relation of Turi, had a little boy named Potikiroroa; this young fellow was sent one day with a message to Uenuku, who was an ariki, or chief high-priest, to let him know that a burnt-offering had been made to the gods, of which Uenuku, as ariki, was to eat part. The little fellow accidentally tripped and fell down in the very doorway of Wharekura, the house of Uenuku, and this being a most unlucky omen, Uenuku was dreadfully irritated, and he laid hold of the little fellow and ate him up without even having the body cooked, and so the poor boy perished.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 14 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Turi was determined to have revenge for this barbarous act, and saw that his best way was to seize Hawepotiki, the little son of Uenuku, and kill him. He ordered the children of his household to whip tops and whirl whizgigs where the boy could see them, but he could not be tempted. At last summer came with its heats; Turi, one very hot day, ordered all the little children to run and bathe in the river Waimatuhirangi, and when little Hawepotiki saw the other lads swimming and playing he was thrown off his guard and ran there too. Turi waylaid him and killed him in a moment, and thus revenged the death of Potikiroroa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 14 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: After killing the poor boy, Turi cut the heart out of his body, which was eaten by himself and his friends; but when a chieftainness named Hotukura sent up a present of baskets of food to the sacred prince Uenuku, some of Turi's friends pushed into the basket of baked sweet potatoes the heart of Te Hawepotiki, cut up and baked too, and so it was carried up and laid before him to eat. Uenuku, who had missed his little boy, sighed when he saw such an excellent feast: 'Poor little Hawepotiki, how he would have liked this, but he now no longer comes running to sit by my side at mealtime' - and he ate the food. Hardly had he ended when a friend came and told him, 'They have made you eat a part of Hawepotiki.' He answered, 'Very well, let it be; he lies in the belly of Toi-te-huatahi' - meaning by this proverb that he would have a fearful revenge - but showed no other sign of feeling.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 14 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: One evening Rongo-rongo, Turi's wife, went out of their house Rangiatea to suckle her little girl and heard Uenuku in his house Wharekura chanting a poem: 'Oh! let the tribes be summoned from the south, oh! let the tribes be summoned from the north; let Ngati-Ruanui come in force, let Ngati-Rongotea's warriors too be there, that we may all our foes destroy and sweep them utterly away. Oh, they ate one far nobler than themselves.' She went back and told her husband, humming it gently over to him, and Turi at once divined the meaning: the poem was meant for him; because he had killed the child of Uenuku they meant to slay him as a payment for the boy, and the lament his wife had heard evinced that they were secretly laying their plans of revenge. He started off at once to his father-in-law Toto to get a canoe in which he might escape from his enemies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 14 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: Kupe Slays the Cuttlefish of Muturangi

region.en: Kura-te-au, Tory Channel, Marlborough Sounds (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫拉特奧水道，馬爾堡峽灣（象徵性定位）

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 14, The Emigration of Turi (London 1855)

summary.en: Kupe covets his cousin Hoturapa's wife Kuramarotini: he pretends his line is foul, lets the good-natured cousin dive, cuts the anchor rope and strands him to drown, then flees in the stolen Matahorua and discovers the islands of New Zealand, coasting entirely round them without finding inhabitants - only the birds kokako and tiwaiwaka. At Castle Point a great cuttle-fish flees its cavern before him; in Tory Channel it rears its sucker-armed bulk to engulf the canoe, and Kupe throws over a huge water-calabash; the monster, taking it for the canoe, rears up to crush it, and Kupe severs it in two with his axe - the Wheke-a-Muturangi slain.
summary.zh: 庫佩覬覦表弟霍圖拉帕之妻庫拉馬羅蒂尼：他謊稱釣線被纏，誘好心的表弟潛水解線，趁機砍斷錨繩將其拋棄海中，帶著贓婦駕馬塔霍魯阿號遠遁，發現新西蘭群島並環航一周，未見人煙——只有科卡科與蒂瓦伊瓦卡兩鳥。至城堡角，巨魷自洞穴竄逃；在托里水道它張開吸盤巨臂欲吞獨木舟，庫佩擲下水葫蘆，巨魷誤以為舟，猛撲其上，庫佩趁勢一斧將其劈為兩半——穆圖蘭基之魷就此授首。

sensitivity.note: Monster-slaying episode tied to discovery of Aotearoa; world-serpent tagging is interpretive (octopus as sea-monster).

passages.text: One day Kupe and Hoturapa went out upon the sea to fish together, and when they had anchored the canoe at a convenient place, Kupe let down his line and said to his cousin, 'Hotu', my line is foul of something; do you, like a good young fellow, dive down and release it for me.' Hoturapa said, 'Just give me your line, and let me see if I cannot pull it up for you.' But Kupe answered, 'It's of no use, you cannot do it; you had better give a plunge in at once, and pull it up.' This was a mere stratagem on the part of Kupe, that he might obtain possession of Kuramarotini, who was Hoturapa's wife; however Hoturapa not suspecting this, good-naturedly dived down at once to bring up Kupe's line.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 14 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: As soon as he had made his plunge, Kupe at once cut the rope which was attached to the anchor and paddled off for the shore as fast as he could go, to carry off Hoturapa's wife Kuramarotini. When Hoturapa came up to the surface the canoe was already a long distance from him, and he cried out to Kupe to bring the canoe back to take him in; but Kupe would not listen, brought not back the canoe, and so Hoturapa perished. Kupe then made haste and carried off Kuramarotini, and to escape from the vengeance of the relations of Hoturapa he fled away with her on the ocean in her canoe Matahorua, and discovered the islands of New Zealand, and coasted entirely round them, without finding any inhabitants. He only found two inhabitants in the country, a bird which he named the Kokako, and another bird which he named the Tiwaiwaka; he did not ultimately remain in these islands, but returned to his own country, leaving the openings he had examined in the country as signs that he had been here.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 14 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: As Kupe was proceeding down the east coast of New Zealand and had reached Castle Point, a great cuttle-fish, alarmed at the sight of a canoe with men in it, fled away from a large cavern which exists in the south headland of the cove there; it fled before Kupe in the direction of Raukawa, Cook's Straits. When he arrived at those straits he crossed them to examine the middle islands; seeing the entrance of Awa-iti, now called Tory Channel, running deep up into the land, he turned his canoe in there to explore it; the entrance he named Kura-te-au. Strong as the current was, Kupe stemmed it until he was just surmounting the crown of the rapid. The great cuttle-fish or dragon that had fled from Castle Point, which Kupe named Te Wheke-a-Muturangi, the cuttle-fish of Muturangi, was lying hid in this part of the current; it heard the canoe approaching, and raised its arms above the waters to catch and devour the canoe, men and all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 14 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kupe pondered how he might destroy the terrible monster. He had already found that, although he kept on chopping off portions of its gigantic arms furnished with suckers as it tried to fold them about the canoe to pull it down, the monster was too fierce to care for this; so Kupe seized an immense hollow calabash he had on board to carry his water in, and threw it overboard. Hardly had it touched the water ere the monster flew at it, thinking it was the canoe of Kupe; so it reared its whole body out of the water to press down the huge calabash under it, and Kupe, as he stood in his canoe, being in a most excellent position to cut it with his axe, seized the opportunity, and striking it a tremendous blow, severed it in two and killed it. Several spots upon the east coast are shown where Kupe touched with his canoes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 14 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: Turi Plants Patea: Eight Potatoes, Eight Hundred Baskets
title.zh: 圖里墾帕蒂亞：八薯八百籃

region.zh: 紐西蘭塔拉納基海岸帕蒂亞河

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 14, The Emigration of Turi (London 1855)

summary.en: The Aotea sails east against Kupe's instructions: Potoru's Ririno is dashed on Taputapuatea reef - 'you are as obstinate as Potoru, who persisted in rushing on to his own destruction'. Turi's canoe refits at Rangitahua after dog sacrifices, a child Tutawa is born at sea and fed his first food from the last ninth potato, and at landfall the footprints of the crewman thrown overboard are found on the sand. Turi follows the coast naming harbours from Kawhia to Patea, plants karaka berries all along the route, builds the pa Rangitaawhi, and makes his eight remaining seed potatoes into eight hundred baskets - the harvest of the ancestor of the Whanganui tribes.
summary.zh: 圖里本應向東航向日出之方，卻聽任波托魯向西而行：里里諾號觸礁碎裂，成諺『你像波托魯一樣固執，偏要撞向自取滅亡之處』。奧特亞號在蘭吉塔胡亞島重整，以犬祭神；海上出生的幼子圖塔瓦以最後一枚甘薯行初食禮；登陸沙灘，先見被拋海船員的腳印。圖里沿海岸為各地命名，沿途播下卡卡樹果核，築蘭吉塔維要塞，將僅餘的八枚薯種分切栽種——收成八百籃，此即旺加努伊諸部之祖的功業。

sensitivity.note: Ethnogenesis legend of Whanganui tribes; extensive place-name etymology reproduced selectively.

passages.text: Amongst the chiefs who landed at the mid-ocean island Rangitahua with them was one named Porua, whose canoe was called Te Ririno. They were carrying dogs with them as these would be valuable in the islands for food and skins for warm cloaks; on this island they killed two, Whakapapa-tuakura and Tanga-kakariki; the first they cooked and shared, but the second they cut up raw as an offering for the gods, laid it open before them, built a sacred place and set up pillars for the spirits that they might entirely consume the sacrifice, and took the enchanted apron of the spirits and spread it open, calling on them for an omen and thus removing all ill-luck from the canoes by repeating over them the prayers called Keuenga, Takanga, Whakainuinumanga.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 14 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: When all these ceremonies were ended, a very angry discussion arose between Potoru and Turi as to the direction they should now sail in. Turi persisted in wishing to pursue an easterly course: 'Let us still sail towards the quarter where the sun first flares up'; but Potoru answered, 'I say nay, nay, let us proceed towards that quarter of the heavens in which the sun sets.' Turi reminded him that Kupe, who had visited these islands, had particularly told them to keep the prow ever towards the sunrise; but Potoru persisted, and Turi gave up the point. After they had pursued the westerly course for some time, the canoe Ririno, getting into the surf near some rocks, was lost on a reef they named Taputapuatea, swept by a strong current swiftly running on to the realms of death, and dashed to pieces - hence the proverb to the present day: 'You are as obstinate as Potoru, who persisted in rushing on to his own destruction.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 14 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the Ririno had been lost, Turi in the Aotea pursued his course towards the quarter of the rising sun; whilst they were yet in mid-ocean a child whom he named Tutawa was born to Turi. They had then but nine sweet potatoes left, and Turi took one, leaving now but eight, and offered it as a sacrifice to the spirits, touching with it the palate of little Tutawa, born in mid-ocean, at the same time repeating the fitting prayers. When they drew near the shore, one of the crew, named Tuanui-a-te-ra, was very disobedient and insolent, and Turi, getting exceedingly provoked, threw him overboard into the sea. They also foolishly threw their old red head-ornaments, named Pohutukawa, into the sea, thinking wrongly that the red things they saw in such abundance on the shore were similar ornaments. At length the Aotea is run up on the beach, the wearied voyagers spring out on the sands, and the first thing they remark are the footprints of a man; they run to examine them and find them to be those of Tuanui-a-te-ra, whom Turi had shortly before thrown overboard - there can be no doubt, for some of the footprints are crooked, exactly suiting the deformed foot he had.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 14 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Turi, having rested after his voyage, determined to seek the river Patea which Kupe had described to him, leaving his canoe Aotea in the harbour he named after it. He travelled along the coast-line from Aotea to Patea, having sent one party before him under Pungarehu, ordering them to plant the stones of the karaka-tree berries which they had brought, all along their route, in order that so valuable an article of food might be introduced into these islands. He gave names to the places as he came: at Kawhia, the awhinga of Turi; Marokopa, where he wound round; Waitara, from his wide fording steps; Mokau, where he slept; Manga-ti, where the enchanted garment Hunokiko was spread out; Hongihongi, where he smelt the soil; Tapuwae, the footsteps of Turi; Oakura, from the bright redness of the cloak; Waingongoro, where Turi snored; Ohingahape, after the crooked foot of Tuanui-a-te-ra. At length he reached the river Kupe had described; there he built a pa which he named Rangitaawhi, erected a post Whakatopea, built a house Matangirie, laid down a threshold Paepaehakehake, a storehouse Paeahua, and dug a well Parara-ki-te-uru. The chant they sang as they dug: 'Break up our goddess mother, break up the ancient goddess earth; we speak of you, oh earth, but do not you disturb the plants we have brought hither from Hawaiki the noble; it was Maui who scraped the earth in heaps round the sides in Kuratau.' They had but eight seed potatoes, but divided these into small pieces put separately into the ground; when the shoots sprang up Turi made the place sacred with prayers and incantations, the name of which was Ahuaroa, lest any one should venture there and hurt the plants. Then harvest-time came: they gathered in the crop of sweet potatoes and found they had eight hundred baskets of them. Rongo-rongo was the name of his principal wife, and their children sprang the tribes of Ngati-Apa-nui and Ngati-Ruanui.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 14 (1855); not verbatim.
